overview: Caching in PySpark stores the materialized result of a DataFrame (or RDD) in memory (and optionally on disk) so that subsequent actions reuse the cached partitions instead of recomputing the entire lineage.
The `cache()` method is a convenience alias for `persist()` with the default storage level, which for DataFrames is `MEMORY_AND_DISK` and for raw RDDs is `MEMORY_ONLY`.
Caching is most valuable when the same DataFrame is referenced by multiple actions, breaking Spark's habit of recomputing lazy transformations from the source every time.
learningObjectives: Understand what `cache()` does, that it is lazy, and when it is materialized.
Identify the scenarios where caching improves performance versus when it wastes memory.
Learn how to verify caching in the Spark UI and how to release cached data with `unpersist()`.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Caching is the process of marking a DataFrame or RDD to be retained in the executors' storage memory after its first computation, so that the materialized partitions can be reused across multiple actions without re-executing the upstream DAG. `cache()` is shorthand for `persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)` for the Dataset/DataFrame API.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine you bake a complex cake (an expensive DataFrame) and several people want a slice. Without caching, you'd bake the entire cake from scratch each time someone asks. Caching means you bake it once, keep it on the counter, and just hand out slices for every later request.
coreConcept.historicalContext: In-memory caching was one of the headline features that distinguished Spark from Hadoop MapReduce in 2010. MapReduce wrote intermediate results to HDFS between every stage, while Spark's RDD abstraction allowed iterative and interactive workloads to keep data in RAM. The DataFrame API later changed the default cache level from `MEMORY_ONLY` (RDDs) to `MEMORY_AND_DISK` to avoid silent recomputation when memory ran out.

whyItMatters.business: Reusing cached data accelerates iterative analytics, ML training loops, and interactive notebooks, directly reducing the time analysts and data scientists wait for results and lowering cluster runtime billing.
whyItMatters.engineering: Caching eliminates redundant recomputation of expensive lineages (joins, aggregations, UDFs), turning a multi-action pipeline that re-reads source data N times into one that materializes once.
whyItMatters.scalability: Properly cached intermediate datasets let pipelines scale to more downstream consumers without linearly multiplying upstream I/O and shuffle cost, but over-caching can exhaust executor memory and trigger spilling or eviction.
whyItMatters.cost: Avoiding repeated scans of large source tables (e.g., on S3 or HDFS) reduces I/O, network, and compute cost; conversely, over-caching forces larger or more numerous executors, increasing cost.
whyItMatters.reliability: Using `MEMORY_AND_DISK` (the DataFrame default) means cached partitions that don't fit in memory spill to disk and are recovered correctly, avoiding the silent recomputation surprises of `MEMORY_ONLY`.

coreComponents.name: cache() method
coreComponents.definition: A method on DataFrame/RDD that marks it for storage using the default storage level.
coreComponents.purpose: Provide a simple, one-call way to request that a dataset be retained across actions.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Set the storage level (MEMORY_AND_DISK for DataFrames) and register the dataset with the BlockManager; does not itself trigger computation.

coreComponents.name: BlockManager / Storage Memory
coreComponents.definition: The executor-side subsystem that stores cached partitions as blocks in the unified memory region reserved for storage.
coreComponents.purpose: Hold materialized partitions in RAM (or disk) and serve them to subsequent tasks.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Track which blocks are cached, evict blocks under memory pressure using LRU, and spill to disk when the level permits.
coreComponents.examples: Visible in the Spark UI 'Storage' tab as cached RDDs/DataFrames with fraction cached and size in memory/disk

coreComponents.name: First Action (Materialization Trigger)
coreComponents.definition: The action (count, collect, write, etc.) whose execution actually computes and stores the cached partitions.
coreComponents.purpose: Because cache() is lazy, the cache is only populated when an action forces the DAG to run.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Execute the lineage once, write partitions into storage memory, and make them available for reuse.
coreComponents.examples: df_filtered.count() materializes the cache; later df_filtered.show() reads from it

internalWorking: Calling `cache()` only sets a flag and a storage level on the logical plan; no data is read or stored yet because the call is lazy like all transformations.

When the first action runs, Spark executes the DAG, and as each partition is computed it is written into the executor's storage memory (and spilled to disk if using MEMORY_AND_DISK and memory is insufficient).
On subsequent actions, the optimizer recognizes the cached node (an InMemoryRelation in the physical plan) and reads partitions from the BlockManager instead of recomputing the upstream operators.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Source -> Transformations (lineage) -> cache() marks node -> First Action materializes -> Partitions stored in BlockManager (memory/disk) -> Subsequent Actions read from cache (InMemoryRelation)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 2. df.cache() marks the result for storage but reads nothing yet.
3. df.count() (first action) executes the full join+aggregation once and stores resulting partitions in memory across executors.
4. df.filter(...).show() and df.write.parquet(...) reuse the cached partitions instead of re-running the join and aggregation.
5. When the DataFrame is no longer needed, df.unpersist() releases the blocks so memory can be reclaimed.

keyTerminology.meaning: Transformations (including cache()) are recorded but not executed until an action triggers computation.
keyTerminology.importance: Explains why a DataFrame is not actually cached until the first action runs against it.

keyTerminology.meaning: The graph of transformations Spark records to recompute a dataset from its source.
keyTerminology.importance: Caching short-circuits re-execution of the lineage; without a cache, every action replays it from scratch.

keyTerminology.meaning: The physical plan node Spark substitutes for a cached DataFrame so reads come from the cache.
keyTerminology.importance: Seeing InMemoryRelation in explain() confirms the cache is being used by a query.

importantConcepts.concept: cache() is lazy, materialization is eager-on-first-action
importantConcepts.explanation: cache() returns immediately without storing data. Only the first action populates the cache. A common idiom is to call df.count() right after cache() to force materialization deterministically before timed downstream work.

Caching trades memory for compute. If the lineage is cheap (a single scan) or the data is read only once, recomputation may be cheaper than occupying memory; if the lineage is expensive and reused, caching wins.

variationsAndTypes: **cache():** Uses the default level; MEMORY_AND_DISK for DataFrames, MEMORY_ONLY for RDDs.
**persist(StorageLevel):** Lets you choose a specific level (MEMORY_ONLY, DISK_ONLY, serialized, replicated, off-heap) for finer control.
**SQL CACHE TABLE:** `CACHE TABLE t` eagerly caches a table in Spark SQL; `CACHE LAZY TABLE t` makes it lazy, mirroring the DataFrame behavior.
advantages: **Eliminates Recomputation:** Reused DataFrames skip re-executing expensive joins, aggregations, and UDFs across multiple actions.
**Faster Iterative Workloads:** ML training loops and interactive exploration become dramatically faster when the working dataset is cached.
**Reduces Source I/O:** Avoids repeatedly reading large source files from object storage or HDFS.
**Simple API:** A single cache() call delivers reuse benefits without manual checkpoint management.
disadvantages: **Memory Pressure:** Cached blocks consume storage memory, reducing what is available for shuffles and execution, which can cause spilling or OOM.
**Over-Caching Waste:** Caching DataFrames used only once wastes memory and provides no benefit.
**Eviction Surprises:** Under memory pressure, LRU eviction can drop blocks, causing partial recomputation that's hard to diagnose.
**Stale Memory Footprint:** Forgetting to unpersist leaves blocks resident, starving later stages of memory.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Cache when a non-trivial DataFrame is referenced by two or more actions, in iterative algorithms, or when interactively exploring the same intermediate result repeatedly.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid caching when a DataFrame is consumed by exactly one action, when its lineage is a single cheap scan, or when memory is tight and the recompute cost is low.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Caching is like photocopying a frequently referenced document and keeping the copies on your desk. The first copy costs effort (the first action), but every later read is instant. If you photocopy documents you'll only read once, you just clutter your desk (waste memory).

commonMisconceptions.myth: Calling cache() immediately loads the DataFrame into memory.
commonMisconceptions.reality: cache() is lazy; nothing is stored until the first action runs. The DataFrame is only materialized on the first count/collect/write that touches it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: cache() and persist() are different operations.
commonMisconceptions.reality: cache() is simply persist() with the default storage level. For DataFrames that level is MEMORY_AND_DISK, not MEMORY_ONLY.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Cache size grows with data volume and parallelism; ensure storage memory fraction and executor memory are sized so cached blocks don't crowd out execution memory and cause excessive spilling.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Prefer MEMORY_AND_DISK so partitions that overflow RAM spill to disk rather than being silently evicted and recomputed. Cached data is still fault tolerant via lineage if a block is lost.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: If a cached partition is lost (e.g., executor failure), Spark recomputes it from lineage. Caching does not replace checkpointing for breaking very long lineages.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Use the Spark UI Storage tab to confirm what fraction of each cached dataset is in memory versus disk, and watch for blocks that are only partially cached.
productionConsiderations.security: Cached blocks reside in executor memory and local disk; on multi-tenant clusters ensure disk-spilled blocks are protected by encryption-at-rest and proper directory permissions.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Caching reduces repeated source scans but inflates required executor memory. Right-size by caching only reused datasets and unpersisting promptly.
productionConsiderations.performance: Materialize the cache deterministically (e.g., df.cache(); df.count()) before timed downstream stages, and consider serialized levels to fit more data at the cost of CPU.

codeExamples.title: Basic cache() with a reused DataFrame
codeExamples.overview: Shows how caching a filtered, joined DataFrame avoids recomputing the lineage for multiple downstream actions.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("CacheDemo").getOrCreate()

orders = spark.read.parquet("s3://data/orders")
customers = spark.read.parquet("s3://data/customers")

# Expensive lineage: join + filter
enriched = (orders.join(customers, "customer_id")
                  .filter(orders.amount > 100))

# Mark for caching (lazy - nothing happens yet)
enriched.cache()

# First action materializes the cache
print("Row count:", enriched.count())

# These reuse the cached partitions instead of re-joining
enriched.groupBy("country").sum("amount").show()
enriched.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("s3://data/enriched")

# Release when done
enriched.unpersist()
codeExamples.breakdown: The join+filter is an expensive lineage. cache() marks it but does nothing until enriched.count() runs, which materializes partitions into storage memory. The subsequent groupBy and write read from the cache rather than re-executing the join. unpersist() frees the memory afterward.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Row count is printed once; the groupBy aggregation and the parquet write both run quickly because they reuse cached data. The Spark UI Storage tab shows the cached DataFrame with its size in memory.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting that cache() is lazy and assuming the data is already in memory; not calling unpersist() and leaking memory; expecting the cache to persist across separate Spark applications (it does not).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Call .count() immediately after .cache() to force deterministic materialization before timed work. Only cache because there are at least two downstream actions.

codeExamples.title: Verifying the cache and checking storage level
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrates how to confirm a DataFrame is cached, inspect its storage level, and see the InMemoryRelation in the plan.
codeExamples.code:
df = spark.read.parquet("s3://data/events").filter("event_type = 'purchase'")

df.cache()
df.count()  # materialize

# Confirm it is cached
print(df.is_cached)  # True

# Inspect the storage level (MEMORY_AND_DISK for DataFrame default)
print(df.storageLevel)
# StorageLevel(True, True, False, True, 1)
#   useDisk=True, useMemory=True, useOffHeap=False, deserialized=True, replication=1

# The physical plan shows InMemoryTableScan over an InMemoryRelation
df.filter("amount > 50").explain()

# Free it
df.unpersist(blocking=True)
print(df.is_cached)  # False
codeExamples.breakdown: df.is_cached confirms the cache flag. df.storageLevel prints the resolved StorageLevel; for the DataFrame default cache() it is MEMORY_AND_DISK (useDisk=True, useMemory=True, deserialized=True, replication=1). explain() reveals InMemoryTableScan, proving downstream queries hit the cache. unpersist(blocking=True) waits for the blocks to be removed.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: is_cached prints True, then the StorageLevel string, then a physical plan containing InMemoryTableScan, and finally is_cached prints False after unpersist.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Reading storageLevel before an action makes the level look set but no data is cached; assuming the default cache level is MEMORY_ONLY (it is MEMORY_AND_DISK for DataFrames).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use explain() to verify the optimizer is actually substituting an InMemoryRelation; if not, the cache may not be reused due to a slightly different plan.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retail analytics team runs several daily reports (revenue by region, top products, churn-risk segments) all derived from the same expensive enriched-transactions DataFrame built by joining orders, customers, and products. Recomputing the join for each report wastes hours of cluster time.
endToEndExample.inputData: Three Parquet datasets in object storage: orders (~500M rows), customers (~20M rows), and products (~1M rows), partitioned by date.
endToEndExample.architecture: A Spark batch job on a YARN/Kubernetes cluster reads the three sources, builds one enriched DataFrame, caches it with MEMORY_AND_DISK, then runs multiple report actions against the cached result before unpersisting.
processingSteps: 1. Read orders, customers, and products from Parquet.
2. Join them and apply common filters to build the `enriched` DataFrame (the expensive shared lineage).
3. Call enriched.cache() and then enriched.count() to materialize the cache once.
4. Run report 1 (revenue by region), report 2 (top products), and report 3 (churn segments), each reusing the cache.
5. Write each report to its output location.
6. Call enriched.unpersist() to release the storage memory before the next pipeline stage.
endToEndExample.output: Three report outputs written to storage, each produced quickly from the single cached enriched DataFrame instead of three independent re-joins.
endToEndExample.monitoring: The Spark UI Storage tab shows the cached enriched DataFrame fully resident; the SQL tab shows downstream reports reading from InMemoryRelation. Job duration drops because the join stage runs once.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If executors lack memory, MEMORY_AND_DISK spills overflow partitions to disk rather than failing; lost blocks are recomputed from lineage. If caching causes excessive spill, reduce cached columns or switch to a serialized level.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Total pipeline runtime falls substantially because the costly multi-way join and filter are computed once and reused across three reports, lowering both wall-clock time and cluster cost.

industryUseCases.problem: Iterative ML feature pipelines repeatedly scan the same large enriched viewing-history dataset across many training iterations and feature transformations.
industryUseCases.solution: Cache the cleaned, joined feature DataFrame (MEMORY_AND_DISK) so each iteration and downstream model reads from memory rather than re-reading and re-joining source data.
industryUseCases.benefits: Drastically faster training loops and feature experiments, fewer redundant scans of multi-terabyte source data, and lower cluster cost.

industryUseCases.problem: A single curated trips DataFrame feeds many simultaneous dashboards and aggregations, and recomputing it per query is expensive.
industryUseCases.solution: Build the curated trips DataFrame once and cache it for the duration of the batch session so all aggregations reuse it.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consistent, fast dashboard refreshes and reduced load on the upstream data lake.

industryUseCases.problem: Regulatory reports apply dozens of aggregations to the same enriched positions dataset, and re-reading and re-joining for each is too slow within the reporting window.
industryUseCases.solution: Cache the enriched positions DataFrame after the join, force materialization with count(), then run all regulatory aggregations against the cache, unpersisting when finished.
industryUseCases.benefits: Reports complete within the regulatory SLA window and use predictable memory, avoiding repeated expensive joins.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Cache footprint scales with input size and the number of cached columns. To scale, prune columns before caching, cache only the reused subset, and ensure spark.memory.storageFraction leaves room for both storage and execution memory in the unified memory model.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Cached blocks are not durable; on executor loss Spark recomputes lost partitions from lineage. For pipelines with very long lineages, combine caching with checkpointing to truncate recomputation cost on failure.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Cache lives within a single Spark application's executors and does not survive application restarts. For cross-application reuse, persist the materialized result to storage (e.g., a Delta/Parquet table) instead of relying on in-memory cache.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Because the cache is ephemeral, recovery relies on the durable source data and lineage. Ensure source datasets and any checkpoints are backed up; cache itself needs no DR strategy.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Materialize deterministically with an action after cache(); select only needed columns before caching; consider MEMORY_ONLY_SER to fit more data with lower GC pressure; and verify InMemoryTableScan appears in plans to confirm reuse.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Cache only DataFrames consumed by multiple actions; unpersist as soon as they are no longer needed to release executors' memory; avoid over-provisioning memory to hold caches that provide little reuse benefit.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Disk-spilled cached blocks land in local executor directories; enable local disk encryption and restrict directory permissions on shared clusters. In-memory caches inherit the application's security context.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track the Storage tab for fraction cached, memory vs disk size, and partially cached datasets. Alert on high spill metrics or on caches that never reach full residency, which indicate undersized memory.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Caching does not alter data; however, caching a non-deterministic DataFrame (e.g., with random sampling or current_timestamp) freezes a single realization, which can be desirable for consistency across actions or a subtle bug if recomputation occurs.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Watch executor logs for 'Not enough space to cache' and 'Will not store' warnings indicating blocks could not be cached; alert on frequent block eviction and recomputation.

recommendedPractices: **Cache only reused DataFrames:** Apply cache() when a non-trivial result is read by two or more actions.
**Force materialization deterministically:** Follow cache() with a cheap action like count() before timed downstream work.
**Always unpersist:** Release cached datasets with unpersist() once they are no longer needed.
**Prune before caching:** Select only required columns (and filter) before caching to shrink the memory footprint.
engineeringStandards: Document why each cache exists and which downstream actions justify it.
Pair every cache() with a corresponding unpersist() in the same logical scope.
Verify cache reuse with explain() (look for InMemoryTableScan) rather than assuming it.
designRecommendations: Cache at the point of maximum reuse and minimum size (after filters/projections, before fan-out).
Prefer MEMORY_AND_DISK (the default) over MEMORY_ONLY to avoid silent recomputation under memory pressure.
For very long lineages reused across failures, combine caching with checkpointing.
namingConventions: Name cached DataFrames to signal they are materialized, e.g., enriched_cached or features_cached.
Comment the cache() call with the count of expected downstream consumers.
documentationStandards: Record the chosen storage level and the rationale for caching each dataset.
Note expected cached size and the executors' storage memory budget.
Document the unpersist point in the pipeline lifecycle.
testingStrategies: Compare job runtime and Spark UI stage counts with and without caching to confirm benefit.
Inspect the Storage tab in tests to ensure datasets reach full residency.
Run with reduced executor memory to verify graceful spilling rather than OOM.

commonMistakes.mistake: Caching a DataFrame that is used by only one action.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers cache defensively, assuming it always helps.
commonMistakes.impact: Wastes storage memory, can trigger spilling or eviction of useful blocks, and provides zero reuse benefit while adding overhead to write into the cache.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Only cache when there are at least two downstream actions or an iterative loop reusing the data.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming cache() immediately stores the data.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The method name suggests an eager operation, but cache() is lazy.
commonMistakes.impact: Timing measurements are misleading and the first action that touches the DataFrame pays the full materialization cost unexpectedly.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Trigger an action (e.g., count()) right after cache() to materialize it deterministically.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It's easy to forget cleanup, especially in long-running sessions.
commonMistakes.impact: Cached blocks remain resident, starving later stages of execution memory and causing spills or OOM as the application accumulates caches.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Unpersist each cached DataFrame as soon as its reuse window ends; in notebooks, unpersist before caching new large datasets.

comparisonSection.explanation: cache() always uses the default level (MEMORY_AND_DISK for DataFrames, MEMORY_ONLY for RDDs). persist() lets you pick any level explicitly. They are otherwise identical; cache() is just sugar over persist() with the default.

Caching spends memory to avoid repeated compute; it wins when the lineage is expensive and reused. Recomputing spends CPU/I/O each action; it wins when the lineage is cheap (single scan) or the data is read only once.
DataFrame cache() materializes only on the first action, while SQL `CACHE TABLE t` is eager and materializes immediately (use `CACHE LAZY TABLE` for lazy SQL behavior).

beginnerQuestions.question: What does cache() do in PySpark and is it lazy or eager?
beginnerQuestions.answer: cache() marks a DataFrame to be stored in memory (and disk) so it can be reused across multiple actions without recomputing its lineage. It is lazy: nothing is stored until the first action triggers materialization.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize the lazy nature and the reuse-across-actions purpose. Mention that the first count/collect/write populates the cache.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between cache() and persist()?
beginnerQuestions.answer: cache() is shorthand for persist() using the default storage level. For DataFrames that default is MEMORY_AND_DISK; for raw RDDs it is MEMORY_ONLY. persist() additionally lets you specify any StorageLevel.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The key correction interviewers look for is that the DataFrame default is MEMORY_AND_DISK, not MEMORY_ONLY.

intermediateQuestions.question: When does caching actually help, and when does it hurt?
intermediateQuestions.answer: It helps when a non-trivial DataFrame is reused by multiple actions or in iterative loops, eliminating repeated recomputation. It hurts when a DataFrame is used once, when its lineage is a cheap single scan, or when caching consumes memory needed for execution, causing spilling or eviction.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Frame it as a memory-versus-compute trade-off and stress the 'reused across multiple actions' condition.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you verify a DataFrame is being read from cache, and how do you release it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Check df.is_cached and df.storageLevel, look for InMemoryTableScan/InMemoryRelation in df.explain(), and inspect the Spark UI Storage tab for residency. Release it with df.unpersist() (optionally blocking=True).
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Show familiarity with the practical verification tools and the cleanup method.

advancedQuestions.question: Why might a cached DataFrame still get partially recomputed during a job?
advancedQuestions.answer: Under memory pressure the BlockManager evicts cached blocks using LRU. With MEMORY_ONLY, evicted partitions are silently recomputed from lineage on the next access. Even with MEMORY_AND_DISK, blocks can be dropped if both memory and disk are constrained or an executor is lost.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Discuss LRU eviction, the difference between MEMORY_ONLY and MEMORY_AND_DISK, and executor failure recomputation from lineage.

advancedQuestions.question: How does caching interact with non-deterministic transformations?
advancedQuestions.answer: Caching freezes a single materialization of the DataFrame. If the lineage contains non-deterministic operations (rand(), current_timestamp(), monotonically_increasing_id()), the cached result is one fixed realization. This gives consistency across actions, but if a block is evicted and recomputed it may differ, leading to subtle inconsistencies.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Highlight both the benefit (consistency) and the risk (divergence on recomputation) of caching non-deterministic data.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You have a job that joins two large tables and then produces five separate aggregated reports from the joined result. The job is slow. How do you use caching to speed it up?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Identify the shared expensive lineage (the join). Recognize five downstream actions reuse it. Cache the joined DataFrame, materialize once, then run the five reports against the cache, and unpersist at the end.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Build joined = a.join(b, key), call joined.cache() and joined.count() to materialize once, generate the five reports from joined (each reads from the InMemoryRelation rather than re-joining), then call joined.unpersist(). This turns five joins into one.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the caching strategy for a daily batch pipeline that builds one enriched dataset feeding many downstream aggregations on a memory-constrained cluster.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Project and filter to the minimal needed columns/rows, then cache the enriched DataFrame with MEMORY_AND_DISK so overflow spills rather than evicts. Materialize with count(), run all aggregations, then unpersist.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: MEMORY_AND_DISK avoids silent recomputation but uses local disk and adds serialization on spill. Caching more columns increases reuse benefit but raises memory pressure and risk of eviction.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Tune executor memory and spark.memory.storageFraction; prune columns aggressively; if reuse spans multiple applications, materialize to a Delta/Parquet table instead of relying on in-memory cache.

How do you force a cache to materialize immediately?
What happens to a cached block when an executor dies?
How is caching different from checkpointing?
Does the cache survive across separate Spark applications?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: cache() lazily marks a DataFrame to be stored (MEMORY_AND_DISK by default) so it is reused across actions instead of recomputed from its lineage.
keyConcepts: cache() = persist(MEMORY_AND_DISK) for DataFrames, MEMORY_ONLY for RDDs.
Lazy: materialized on the first action.
Reuse across multiple actions is the win condition.
interviewPoints: DataFrame cache default is MEMORY_AND_DISK, not MEMORY_ONLY.
cache() is lazy; first action materializes.
Only cache when reused across multiple actions.
LRU eviction can cause partial recomputation.
quickNotes: cache() is just persist() with the default storage level.
Call count() after cache() to materialize deterministically.
Over-caching crowds out execution memory and triggers spills.
Cache is per-application and ephemeral; persist to storage for cross-app reuse.
Lost cached blocks are recomputed from lineage, not from a durable store.

keyTakeaways: cache() is shorthand for persist() with the default storage level, which is MEMORY_AND_DISK for DataFrames and MEMORY_ONLY for RDDs.
Caching is lazy: the DataFrame is only materialized into storage memory on the first action, so call count() to force it deterministically.
Caching pays off only when a non-trivial DataFrame is reused across multiple actions or iterations; otherwise it wastes memory.
Under memory pressure, blocks are evicted by LRU and may be recomputed from lineage, so prefer MEMORY_AND_DISK to avoid silent recomputation.
Always unpersist() cached DataFrames when their reuse window ends to free executor memory for execution.
